aciklama: Learn about the life of Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in chronological order.

kartlar.baslik: The Age of Jahiliyyah and the Quraysh
kartlar.icerik:
Prophet Muhammad was born in the 6th century in Mecca, in the Hejaz region of the Arabian Peninsula. The peninsula was organized around tribes and lacked political unity. Grave injustices occurred, including blood feuds, the slave trade, and the burial of baby girls alive. Islamic sources refer to this period as Jahiliyyah (the period of living without the guidance of revelation).

Religiously, idolatry was dominant. There were as many as 360 idols in the Kaaba, the chief among them Hubal, Lat, Manat, and Uzza. There were also a small number of Hanifs (people who sought the path of monotheism followed by Prophet Ibrahim or rejected idolatry).

The Quraysh tribe, which governed Mecca, enjoyed great prestige because it administered the Kaaba. The clan of Banu Hashim, to which Prophet Muhammad belonged, was responsible for providing pilgrims with water and food. His father Abdullah and his mother Aminah belonged to this established family.
kartlar.vurgu: There were 360 idols in the Kaaba · Prophet Muhammad belonged to the Banu Hashim clan of the Quraysh

kartlar.baslik: The Event of the Elephant (around 570 CE)
kartlar.icerik:
Shortly before Prophet Muhammad was born, Abraha, the governor of Yemen, set out to destroy the Kaaba with a large army equipped with elephants. When the army approached Mecca, the elephant at the front refused to advance.

As recounted in Surah al-Fil (105) of the Quran, Allah sent birds called ababil, which destroyed the army by pelting it with stones.

Reports relate that Abdul Muttalib, a respected figure in Mecca, replied to Abraha in words to this effect: 'I am the owner of the camels; the owner of the Kaaba will protect it.' This is a well-known report showing awareness that Allah is the true owner of the Kaaba.
kartlar.vurgu: The Event of the Elephant is recounted in Surah al-Fil (105) of the Quran

kartlar.baslik: Birth and Years with His Wet Nurse (around 571 CE)
kartlar.icerik:
Prophet Muhammad was born on a Monday morning in the Banu Hashim quarter of Mecca, approximately 50–55 days after the Event of the Elephant. His father, Abdullah, had died in Medina before he was born. His grandfather Abdul Muttalib named him 'Muhammad.'

According to the custom of the time, children were entrusted to wet nurses so that they would learn eloquent Arabic. Halimah bint Abi Dhu'ayb of the Banu Sa'd ibn Bakr tribe took him into her care. Prophet Muhammad stayed with Halimah for approximately four years and learned the eloquent Arabic of Hawazin during this time.

His milk siblings were Abdullah, Unaysah, and Shayma.
kartlar.vurgu: His father died before he was born · He learned eloquent Arabic while living with his wet nurse Halimah

kartlar.baslik: Orphanhood: The Deaths of His Mother and Grandfather
kartlar.icerik:
When Prophet Muhammad was 6, his mother Aminah took him to visit his relatives in Medina. On their return journey, she died in the village of Abwa, between Mecca and Medina.

He spent two years receiving his grandfather Abdul Muttalib's special affection, but his grandfather also died when he was 8. On his deathbed, Abdul Muttalib appointed his son Abu Talib as the child's guardian.

Abu Talib and his wife Fatimah bint Asad cared for him like a second set of parents. The Quran speaks of his orphanhood in the context of Allah's protection: 'Did He not find you an orphan and give you shelter?' (ad-Duha 93:6)
kartlar.vurgu: His mother died when he was 6 and his grandfather when he was 8 · His uncle Abu Talib became his guardian

kartlar.icerik:
At the age of 9–12, he joined a trade caravan with his uncle Abu Talib and traveled to Damascus. He had the opportunity to encounter different cultures.

Over time, Prophet Muhammad became so well known for his honesty and trustworthiness that society gave him the title 'al-Amin' (the trustworthy).

Around 590 CE, after a Yemeni man suffered an injustice, tribal representatives gathered at the home of Abdullah ibn Jud'an and pledged to protect those who were wronged. This agreement was called 'Hilf al-Fudul' (the Alliance of the Virtuous). Prophet Muhammad, who was a young man at the time, also took part. Reports relate that the Prophet ﷺ said he would join this alliance if called upon to do so even during the Islamic period.
kartlar.vurgu: 'al-Amin': the title meaning 'the trustworthy,' given to him spontaneously by Meccan society

kartlar.baslik: Marriage to Khadijah and the Reconstruction of the Kaaba
kartlar.icerik:
At the age of 25, Prophet Muhammad earned the trust to lead the trade caravan of Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, a widowed businesswoman, to Damascus (around 595 CE). Khadijah proposed marriage, and Prophet Muhammad accepted. They had six children from this marriage.

Khadijah was the person who comforted him when he received the first revelation and was his greatest supporter. She holds the honor of being the first woman to become Muslim.

When he was 35, the Kaaba was rebuilt (605 CE). A dispute arose among the tribes over who would place the Black Stone (the black stone located at a corner of the Kaaba) in position. Prophet Muhammad brought a large cloth and placed the stone in its center. He had the tribal representatives hold the corners of the cloth, and he placed the stone in position himself. In this way, he prevented a major conflict.
kartlar.vurgu: Khadijah: the first woman to believe · Prophet Muhammad placed the Black Stone in position

kartlar.baslik: The First Revelation and the First Muslims (610 CE)
kartlar.icerik:
When Prophet Muhammad was 40, he encountered Jibril during Ramadan in the Cave of Hira on Mount Nur, where he often withdrew into seclusion to reflect. The angel pressed him and said, 'Read!' Then the first five verses of Surah al-Alaq were revealed: 'Read in the name of your Lord who created!'

Prophet Muhammad returned home frightened, with his hands trembling. Khadijah wrapped him up and comforted him. Her cousin Waraqah ibn Nawfal said that the angel who had come was Jibril.

The first Muslims:
• Khadijah — the first among women
• Ali — the first among children (approximately 10 years old)
• Abu Bakr — the first among free men
• Zayd ibn Harithah — the first among freed people

For the first three years, the call to Islam was carried out in secret. The house of Arqam ibn Abi al-Arqam became known as Dar al-Arqam (the house of Arqam; the first center for learning and gathering).
kartlar.vurgu: 'Read in the name of your Lord who created!' (al-Alaq 96:1) — the first command of Islam

kartlar.baslik: The Public Call, Persecution, and Migration to Abyssinia (613–616 CE)
kartlar.icerik:
In 613 CE, the Prophet ﷺ climbed Mount Safa and asked, 'If I told you that an enemy army was behind this mountain, would you believe me?' When the Quraysh replied, 'Yes,' he called on them to heed Allah's warning. Abu Lahab left in anger; Surah al-Masad, also known as Surah Lahab, was revealed in response.

The Quraysh's persecution was directed especially at vulnerable and enslaved Muslims:
• Bilal al-Habashi: He was tortured by having a large stone placed on his chest; Abu Bakr bought and freed him
• Sumayyah: She was martyred by Abu Jahl—she was the first martyr of Islam

In 615–616 CE, when the persecution became unbearable, Muslims migrated to Abyssinia. Approximately 15 people set out in the first group and approximately 100 in the second. Ja'far ibn Abi Talib recited verses from Surah Maryam before the Negus. The Negus did not return the Muslims and provided them with a safe environment.
kartlar.vurgu: Sumayyah was the first martyr of Islam · Abu Bakr freed Bilal

kartlar.baslik: The Boycott, the Year of Sorrow, and Isra and Mi'raj (616–622 CE)
kartlar.icerik:
From 616 to 619 CE, the Quraysh imposed a comprehensive boycott on the Banu Hashim. The Muslims were confined for approximately three years in the valley of Shi'b Abi Talib (the quarter or valley of Abu Talib), suffering severe hunger and deprivation.

619 CE, the Year of Sorrow: His uncle and protector Abu Talib died, followed by his wife Khadijah. His social protection in Mecca was greatly weakened.

The journey to Ta'if (619 CE): He and Zayd ibn Harithah went to the Thaqif tribe, who had them pelted with stones. The Prophet ﷺ did not curse them.

Isra and Mi'raj (620/621 CE): Isra is described as the night journey from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa; Mi'raj is the ascent from there to the heavens and exalted realms. The most important outcome was that the five daily prayers were made obligatory. Initially prescribed as 50 prayers, they were reduced to five after successive reductions, on the advice of Musa.

The Pledges of Aqabah: A pledge means a promise of loyalty and support. The first pledge was made with 12 people in 621, and the second with 75 people in 622; this process laid the groundwork for the Hijrah.
kartlar.vurgu: The five daily prayers were made obligatory during Isra and Mi'raj · Two great sources of support were lost in the Year of Sorrow

kartlar.baslik: The Assassination Attempt and the Cave of Thawr (622 CE)
kartlar.icerik:
The leaders of the Quraysh gathered at Dar al-Nadwah and decided to kill Muhammad ﷺ. They planned for a young man from each tribe to attack together, so that the blood feud could not be placed on a single tribe.

Allah revealed this plan through Jibril. The Prophet ﷺ had Ali lie in his bed and covered him with his green cloak; the guards at the door could not see him. He and Abu Bakr took refuge in the Cave of Thawr, south of Mecca.

The pursuers came as far as the entrance to the cave. When Abu Bakr became concerned, the Prophet ﷺ said, 'Do not grieve; Allah is with us.' (at-Tawbah 9:40)

They waited in the cave for three nights. Abdullah ibn Urayqit, a trusted guide, was hired to show them the way.
kartlar.vurgu: 'Do not grieve; Allah is with us.' (at-Tawbah 9:40)

kartlar.baslik: Arrival in Quba and Madinah (622 CE)
kartlar.icerik:
After a journey of approximately 8–9 days, the Prophet ﷺ reached Quba. There, Quba Mosque, the first mosque in Islam, was built. The first Friday prayer was performed in the valley of Ranuna.

When he entered Madinah, every tribe was eager to host him. The Prophet ﷺ let his camel go freely, saying, 'Wherever it kneels, I will stay.' The camel knelt at the site of what is now the Prophet's Mosque. Abu Ayyub al-Ansari became his host.

The city of Yathrib came to be known as Madinah. The Hijrah was accepted as the starting point of the Hijri calendar, which was later made official during the time of Umar.
kartlar.vurgu: Quba Mosque is the first mosque built in Islamic history

kartlar.baslik: Building Madinah: The Mosque, Brotherhood, and the Constitution
kartlar.icerik:
Immediately after the arrival in Madinah, three fundamental steps were taken:

1. The Prophet's Mosque: Land was purchased and the mosque was built. The Prophet ﷺ personally carried stones. The Suffah was established beside it as an educational area where Companions who studied there stayed.

2. Brotherhood between the Muhajirun and the Ansar: Each of the Muhajirun who came from Mecca—the Meccans who migrated—was paired in brotherhood with one of the Ansar, the Muslim helpers of Madinah. The Quran praises the Ansar's selflessness, or ithar—the virtue of putting one's brother before oneself even when in need: 'They prefer their brothers over themselves, even when they themselves are in need.' (al-Hashr 59:9)

3. The Constitution of Madinah: This agreement included Muslims and Jewish tribes and provided for freedom of religion, common defense, and the referral of disputes to the Prophet ﷺ.

Also: Inspired by Abdullah ibn Zayd's dream, Bilal al-Habashi became the first muezzin. The qiblah faced Jerusalem for approximately 16–17 months; in the second year after the Hijrah, it was changed to the Kaaba (al-Baqarah 2:144).
kartlar.vurgu: The Constitution of Madinah is one of the earliest written examples of pluralistic governance in history

kartlar.icerik:
On 17 Ramadan, 2 AH / 13 March 624 CE, the first major battle in Islamic history took place.

Muslims: approximately 313 people.
Quraysh: approximately 1,000 people.

That night, the Prophet ﷺ prayed from his heart: 'My Lord! If You do not destroy this group, no one will remain on earth to worship You.' The Muslims gained the upper hand in the battle. Seventy leading Quraysh figures were killed, including Abu Jahl, and 70 people were taken prisoner. Fourteen Muslims were martyred.

Two options were offered to the prisoners: pay a ransom—the price paid for release—or, according to reports, teach 10 Muslims to read and write. This decision is described as a historical example of knowledge being accepted in exchange for freedom.

The Quran states that angels helped in this battle (al-Anfal 8:9).
kartlar.vurgu: Badr: With 313 people, the Muslims defeated the Quraysh army of 1,000—Islam's first victory

kartlar.baslik: The Battles of Uhud and the Trench (625–627 CE)
kartlar.icerik:
The Battle of Uhud (3 AH / 625 CE):
The Quraysh came with approximately 3,000 people; the Muslims numbered approximately 700. At first, the Muslims had the upper hand. However, despite the Prophet's ﷺ command, most of the archers left their positions in pursuit of spoils—property obtained after battle. Khalid ibn al-Walid exploited this opening and attacked from behind. Hamzah was martyred, and the Prophet ﷺ was wounded. Approximately 70 Companions were martyred. The Quran describes this battle as a test of iman.

The Battle of the Trench (5 AH / 627 CE):
A large coalition besieged Madinah. At the suggestion of the Persian Companion Salman al-Farisi, a trench was dug to the north of the city. This was a defensive strategy unfamiliar to the Arabs. During the siege, which lasted approximately 20–27 days, the enemy could not cross; Allah scattered the enemy armies with wind.
kartlar.vurgu: Lesson from Uhud: Disobedience to orders brought defeat · The Trench: Salman's idea saved Medina

kartlar.icerik:
The Prophet ﷺ set out with approximately 1,400–1,500 Companions to perform Umrah. The Quraysh prevented them from entering Mecca. After lengthy negotiations, the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah was signed with Suhayl ibn Amr.

The treaty's main terms were:
• They would return without performing Umrah that year
• They would perform Umrah for three days the following year
• There would be no fighting for 10 years
• Men who came to Medina from Mecca without their guardian's permission would be returned; those who returned to Mecca from Medina would not be returned

At first glance, this return clause seemed to be against the Muslims' interests. Later, the ruling concerning women who emigrated was addressed separately in the Quran (al-Mumtahanah 60:10). Some Companions found the terms difficult, but the Quran described the treaty as 'a clear victory' (al-Fath 48:1). Over the following two years, the number of people who embraced Islam increased greatly compared with previous years.
kartlar.vurgu: The Quran described Hudaybiyyah as 'a clear victory' (al-Fath 48:1)

kartlar.baslik: Khaybar, the Letters, Mu'tah, and the Conquest of Mecca (628–630 CE)
kartlar.icerik:
Khaybar (7 AH / 628 CE): The fortresses of Khaybar, a center of incitement against the Muslims, were conquered.

Letters to Rulers (7 AH): Letters inviting rulers to Islam were sent with the seal 'Muhammad Rasulullah'. The Byzantine Emperor Heraclius responded respectfully but did not embrace iman. The Sasanian Khosrow tore up the letter. It is reported that the Negus, the ruler of Abyssinia, became Muslim.

The Battle of Mu'tah (629 CE): An expedition against the Ghassanids, who had killed the envoy. After three commanders were martyred in succession, Khalid ibn al-Walid took command and successfully withdrew the army. The Prophet ﷺ gave him the title 'Sayfullah' (the sword of Allah).

The Conquest of Mecca (20 Ramadan 8 AH / January 11, 630 CE): After the Quraysh broke the treaty, the Muslims entered Mecca with an army of 10,000. The city was conquered almost without bloodshed. Reports relate that the Prophet ﷺ declared a broad general amnesty and said words meaning, 'Go, you are all free.' The 360 idols in the Kaaba were destroyed.
kartlar.vurgu: The general amnesty at the conquest of Mecca is a great example of mercy and forgiveness

kartlar.baslik: Hunayn, Tabuk, and the Year of Delegations (630 CE)
kartlar.icerik:
Hunayn (630 CE): Seventeen days after the conquest of Mecca, the Hawazin and Thaqif tribes ambushed the Muslim army of 12,000. The army, confident in its numerical superiority, panicked at first (at-Tawbah 9:25). The Prophet ﷺ did not retreat; the Muslims gathered in response to Abbas's call, which rallied the Companions again, and victory was achieved.

The Expedition of Tabuk (630 CE): The last major expedition in which the Prophet ﷺ took part. The 'Army of Hardship' numbered approximately 30,000. Sacrifice: Abu Bakr donated all his wealth, Umar donated half of his, and Uthman contributed a third of the army's needs. There was no battle; the hypocrites (those who appeared to believe despite not believing inwardly) were exposed.

The Year of Delegations (630–632 CE): Arab tribes became Muslim one after another. Surah an-Nasr had given glad tidings of these mass conversions: 'You see people entering the religion of Allah in groups.' (an-Nasr 110:2)
kartlar.vurgu: 'You see people entering the religion of Allah in groups.' (an-Nasr 110:2)

kartlar.baslik: The Farewell Hajj, Sermon, and Passing (632 CE)
kartlar.icerik:
The Farewell Hajj (Dhul-Hijjah 10 AH / March 632 CE): The Prophet's ﷺ first and last Hajj. Approximately 100,000 to 124,000 Muslims participated. The Farewell Sermon was delivered at Jabal ar-Rahmah in Arafat:
• The inviolability of life, property, and honor
• The abolition of interest from the Age of Ignorance
• The rejection of racial superiority: 'Superiority is only through God-consciousness'
• Good treatment of women

During the sermon, al-Ma'idah 5:3 was revealed: 'Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favor upon you.' This verse is one of the most important verses announcing the completion of the religion.

Passing (12 Rabi al-Awwal 11 AH / June 8, 632 CE): The Prophet ﷺ passed away at approximately 63 years of age, with Aisha at his side. In his final days, Abu Bakr led the prayers.

Abu Bakr ascended the pulpit and spoke the historic words: 'Whoever worships Muhammad should know that Muhammad has died. Whoever worships Allah should know that Allah is Ever-Living and does not die.' (Al Imran 3:144)
